analysis.one_liner: Lets people resell devices with their software intact, and bars makers from blocking it by contract.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one representative with no cosponsors, never left the House Judiciary Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend copyright law so that when you sell, lease, or give away a device that runs on software—anything from a printer to a router to a car—you can transfer the software along with it. Companies could not write contracts saying you can't. If the original buyer had a right to security fixes and error corrections, those rights would pass to the new owner. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy and resell used electronics, and people buying secondhand devices, who today often can't legally transfer the software that makes the device work. The bill would also pass along rights to security updates, so a used device could keep getting fixes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Buyers and resellers of used electronics

how_it_helps.text: The owner of a device could transfer an authorized copy of the software that makes it run when selling, leasing, or giving away the device, and this right could not be waived by any agreement [S2][S3].
Any right to receive security or error-correction updates that applied to the original owner would carry over to the new owner, helping secondhand devices stay safe [S2][S3].
The bill preserves copyright protections by barring a seller from keeping an unauthorized copy of the software after the transfer [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Software and device makers, whose business models often treat embedded software as licensed rather than owned—letting them restrict resale, tie devices to subscription fees, or limit updates to first owners.

drawbacks.text: Device makers argue that per-device software licenses fund ongoing updates and security support; allowing transfers could complicate how updates are delivered and undercut revenue that keeps devices patched [S2][S3].
The bill was never analyzed in committee, so questions like how it applies to software tied to online accounts or cloud services were left unanswered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a narrow, well-targeted fix: it extended a long-standing principle—that when you buy something, you own it—to the software inside modern devices, while explicitly blocking sellers from keeping pirate copies. The cost to manufacturers is real but limited, and the benefit to consumers is straightforward. The main weakness is that it died before any hearing, so practical details were never worked through.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee, then a subcommittee, and expired when the two-year Congress ended without ever getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Blake Farenthold introduced the bill in the House on September 18, 2014 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1][S5].
On October 28, 2014, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet, where it stayed [S5].
No cosponsors ever signed on [S4], and no further action was taken before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Device and software makers kept the ability to restrict how embedded software is resold through licensing and contracts, and consumers gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Blake Farenthold
for.what_they_did: Introduced the You Own Devices Act and became its only sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, sent it to its intellectual property subcommittee, and never held a hearing or markup on it.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member of Congress was involved—a Republican sponsor with no cosponsors—so the record shows no partisan pattern either way.

industries.note: Many companies sell hardware with embedded software that is licensed, not owned, so they can bar resale, keep updates for first buyers, or push subscription fees. The bill would override those contract restrictions, cutting into that revenue while giving consumers real ownership of what they buy.
Resellers and secondhand marketplaces could legally transfer working software with a device, making used goods more valuable and useful to buyers.
